nameStory: The 'pennywort' name comes from the plant's distinctive round, coin-shaped leaves that reminded early settlers of copper pennies. 'Marshpennywort' reflects its love of wet places, while 'manyflower' refers to the clusters of tiny blooms that appear in umbrella-like arrangements above the penny-sized leaves.
description: Manyflower marshpennywort is a small aquatic plant that forms low mats in wet, sandy areas. Its most striking feature is the perfectly round, bright green leaves that look like tiny lily pads or coins floating on slender stems. The plant rarely grows more than a few inches tall, spreading horizontally through creeping runners. Despite its delicate appearance, it's a hardy little survivor that can handle both fully submerged and just-damp conditions.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Perfectly circular leaves about the size of a penny or quarter, with a smooth, waxy feel and bright green color. The leaf stem attaches right in the center of the leaf disc, like a tiny green umbrella.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or greenish flowers cluster together in small umbrella-shaped groups (umbels) on stems that rise above the leaves. Individual flowers are barely noticeable but the clusters are distinctive.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, creeping mats that spread along wet ground or float partially submerged. Stems are thin and soft, feeling almost succulent when gently squeezed.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, pale green stems that feel soft and slightly squishy, often rooting at joints where they touch wet soil or shallow water.

habitat: Look for manyflower marshpennywort in wet, sandy areas like pond edges, marshes, and seasonally flooded spots. It thrives in shallow water or on soggy soil that stays consistently moist. In New England, it's quite rare and most likely to be found in protected wetland areas.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as bright green penny-shaped leaves on creeping stems, often forming small colonies in wet areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full leaf development and tiny umbrella-shaped flower clusters appearing above the circular leaves.
seasonality.fall: Plants may persist into early fall in milder areas, though growth slows significantly as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: In most of New England, the plant dies back completely, surviving as underground parts that will regrow the following spring.

funFact: This innocent-looking little plant is actually edible and tastes mildly like parsley - you could literally make a salad out of 'pennies' from your local marsh! However, since it's quite rare in New England and considered threatened in some states, it's better admired than eaten.
confusionNotes: The round, centrally-attached leaves are so distinctive that manyflower marshpennywort is rarely confused with other plants. The closest look-alike might be very young water lily leaves, but pennywort leaves are much smaller and the stems attach differently.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the ivy family (Araliaceae), this plant looks nothing like the ivy we're familiar with. It's also sometimes called 'dollarweed,' especially in warmer climates where it can become a lawn pest, though that's rarely an issue in cooler New England.
compareHints: Among New England's water pennyworts, manyflower marshpennywort has the most perfectly circular leaves and the most obvious umbrella-shaped flower clusters. American water-pennywort has more kidney-shaped leaves with wavy edges, while whorled pennywort has leaves arranged in circles around the stem rather than growing individually from creeping runners.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American water-pennywort can be distinguished from its relatives by its consistently round leaves and preference for the northeastern climate.
Among New England's pennyworts, whorled pennywort is the easiest to identify because of its perfectly circular leaves attached at the center.
Unlike American Water-pennywort which has kidney-shaped or lobed leaves, Sibthorp's Pennywort has perfectly round, unlobed leaves.
Unlike its pennywort relatives in New England, floating marsh pennywort is the only one that forms true floating mats on open water.
**[UNCERTAIN]** Compared to its more common cousin American Water-pennywort, this species likely differs in leaf size, flower arrangement, or specific habitat requirements.
